input:
For the spare motor, the established policy sets the safety stock at 835 units, determined to support a 95% cycle service level over a replenishment lead time of 8 weeks. The safety stock protects against variability in demand during the lead time, rather than covering average demand, which is handled separately.

The mean demand stands at 785 units per week, with a standard deviation of 179 units per week around that mean. Across the full 8 weeks of the lead time, the average demand comes to some 6280 units in total, and this average requirement is what the cycle stock is there to satisfy. The role of the safety stock, by contrast, is to absorb the fluctuation around that average, because in roughly half of all cycles actual demand runs above the mean, and the 835 units soak up that excess up to the specified service level. Bringing the two elements together, the reorder point works out at 7115 units, which is simply the lead-time demand combined with the safety stock, and ordering at this point should ensure that replenishment arrives in good time in most cycles.

Demand has been treated as normally distributed and as independent from one week to the next. The independence assumption is what allows the weekly variability to be combined across the lead time in the manner assumed; a pattern of linked heavy weeks would fall outside this treatment. Seasonal peaks have been excluded from the demand data behind the figure, so the 95% service level is a statement about the modelled demand only. In a peak season the same stock is drawn on under a demand pattern the figure does not describe, and the cover achieved will be lower than the headline level. The figure remains valid while the demand pattern behind it remains unchanged; a shift in mean demand, in weekly variability, or in the lead time would change the safety stock the service level requires, and the policy figure would then be recalculated from the new values.
target:
The spare-motor store holds 835 units as safety stock. The figure is set for a 95% cycle service level against a replenishment lead time of 8 weeks, and it is the stock held against demand variation during that lead time, not against average demand.

Mean demand is 785 units per week, with a standard deviation of 179 units per week. Demand over the 8 weeks of lead time averages 6280 units, and that average is met from cycle stock. The safety stock covers the spread around the average: demand in a lead time runs above its mean in about half of all cycles, and the 835 units absorb the excess up to the stated service level. The reorder point is 7115 units, the lead-time demand and the safety stock together, and an order placed at that point arrives before the safety stock is drawn down in all but the worst cycles the service level admits.

The calculation treats demand as normal and independent between weeks. Independence is what lets the weekly spread combine over the lead time in the way the figure assumes; a run of heavy weeks that are not independent of each other is outside the treatment. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand record behind the figure, and the 95% level is a statement about the modelled demand only. A peak season draws on the same stock under a demand pattern the figure does not describe, and cover in a peak season is lower than the stated level. The figure stands while the demand pattern it rests on stands: a change in mean demand, in the weekly spread, or in the lead time changes the safety stock the service level requires, and the policy figure is then recomputed from the new values rather than adjusted by judgement.
